title: Solomon's Kingdom at Its Height
overview: This chapter describes how Solomon ran his kingdom, how it supplied his court, how prosperous and peaceful it was, and how famous he became for his wisdom.

parts.label: Solomon's top officials (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: Several of these men had served Solomon's father David, and others were sons of Zadok the priest and of a man named Nathan, probably the prophet Nathan who helped Solomon become king, though the chapter does not say so. One official ran forced labor, crews of people made to work on royal building projects, a burden that later helped spark a revolt (1 Kings 12).

parts.label: Twelve districts feed the court (vv. 7-19)
parts.note: Each district supplied the palace for one month a year, a kind of tax paid in food rather than money. Judah does not clearly appear on the list, and many scholars think it may have been treated differently, which could help explain later anger in the north.

parts.label: Peace and plenty (vv. 20-21, 24-25)
parts.note: Picturing the people as countless as sand on the shore echoes God's promise to Abraham, and each family sitting safely under its own vine and fig tree became a classic image of settled, secure life. The claim that kingdoms from the Euphrates River to Egypt paid Solomon tribute is hard to confirm outside the Bible, and historians debate how large his realm really was.

parts.label: Food and horses (vv. 22-23, 26-28)
parts.note: These daily supplies fed the whole court, including officials, guards, servants and guests, not just the king himself. Ancient copies differ on the number of horse stalls (4,000 or 40,000), and a parallel passage in 2 Chronicles gives 4,000.

parts.label: Solomon's famous wisdom (vv. 29-34)
parts.note: His wisdom is measured against the peoples of the East and Egypt, both famous for learning, and against wise men of his day, of whom Ethan and Heman are linked to psalms while the others are unknown. It covered sayings, songs and close study of nature, from the tall cedar to the small hyssop plant on a wall, though most of what he is said to have produced has not survived.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this chapter is simple praise of Solomon's golden age or also quietly hints at trouble ahead, such as his use of forced labor and his huge number of horses, the second being something a law in Deuteronomy 17 tells kings not to pile up.
think: When a society seems peaceful and well supplied, whose work and whose costs are most likely to go unnoticed?
